\chapter{Zero, Halves and Dozens}
\label{ch:cero-y-mitad}
\hlchaptermodality{344}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say cero, el numero, la mitad, la docena and doble, and say why English borrowed the same Arabic word twice, as zero and as cipher.}

Complete ES-C344-doble: count from zero, name the number itself, halve a thing, count it by twelves, and double it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[cero]{cero — zero, the empty one, and the word English borrowed twice}

\label{lesson:ES-C344-cero}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the age, the era}, then \emph{the century}. (\emph{La época}; \emph{el siglo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco — the counting this completes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SE-ro}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{c} before \emph{e} is soft, an \emph{s} across the Americas. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cero} — \textquotedblleft{}zero.\textquotedblright{}

Roman numerals have no zero. You cannot write it: there is no symbol, because there was no idea. Counting started at one, and \emph{nothing} was not a number.

The zero arrived with Arabic mathematics, and it brought its name. Arabic \textbf{ṣifr} meant \emph{empty} — a translation of the Sanskrit \emph{śūnya}, also \emph{empty}. Latin took it as \textbf{zephirum} and \textbf{cifra}, and the two forms went separate ways across Europe.

English ended up borrowing the same Arabic word twice. From \emph{zephirum} through Italian came \textbf{zero}. From \emph{cifra} came \textbf{cipher} — which in older English means a nought, and also a secret code, because Arabic numerals looked like unreadable marks to people used to Roman ones. A \textbf{cipher} can be a nobody, a zero, or a code, and all three are the same borrowed emptiness.

Spanish kept both as well: \emph{cero} is the number, and \textbf{la cifra} is a digit or a figure.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Counting has a floor under it now.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cero}
  \item \emph{cero o uno}
  \item \emph{el número cero}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Arabic \emph{ṣifr} mean? (Empty.) And which two English words came from it? (\emph{Zero} and \emph{cipher}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el número]{el número — the number, and the letter English added by mistake}

\label{lesson:ES-C344-numero}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the century}, then \emph{zero}. (\emph{El siglo}; \emph{cero}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item cero — the one this now counts from.
  \item uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco — what a number names.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{NU-me-ro}, the weight on the first beat, which is why it takes a written accent. Three even, short vowels. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el número} — \textquotedblleft{}the number.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{numerus}, a number. The straight line from Latin to Spanish, with almost nothing happening on the way.

What is worth noticing is what happened in English instead. Latin \emph{numerus} went into French as \emph{nombre}, and English took it as \textbf{number} — with a \textbf{b} that was never in the Latin word. It crept in because \emph{m} followed by \emph{r} is awkward to say, and a \emph{b} slips into the gap without anybody deciding to put it there. English did the same in \textbf{chamber} and \textbf{slumber}.

Spanish never added it. \textbf{Número} keeps the Latin shape exactly, so the Spanish word is closer to the original than the English one is.

The rest of the family is clean. A \textbf{numeral} is the written sign. \textbf{Numerous} means many. To \textbf{enumerate} is to go through one by one. And something \textbf{innumerable} cannot be counted at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word for the count itself, on top of the counting.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el número}
  \item \emph{el número dos}
  \item \emph{¿cuál es el número?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where did the \emph{b} in English \emph{number} come from? (It slipped in between \emph{m} and \emph{r}; the Latin never had it.) And which language kept the Latin shape? (Spanish — \emph{número}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la mitad]{la mitad — the half, built from middle with an ending you own}

\label{lesson:ES-C344-mitad}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{zero}, then \emph{the number}. (\emph{Cero}; \emph{el número}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item -dad — the ending, for the fourth time.
  \item mediodía, medianoche — the same middle, doing the clock.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mi-TAD}, the weight on the second beat. The final \emph{-d} is very soft and often fades away entirely. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la mitad} — \textquotedblleft{}the half.\textquotedblright{}

Two things you already own are inside it.

The ending is \textbf{-dad}, from Latin \textbf{-tātem} — the one you have met in \textbf{verdad}, \textbf{ciudad} and \textbf{edad}, and which English turns into \textbf{-ty}. It makes an abstract noun: \emph{the state of being such-and-such}.

The stem is \textbf{medius}, \emph{middle} — the same \emph{medius} sitting in \textbf{mediodía} and \textbf{medianoche}, the middle of the day and the middle of the night.

Put them together and Latin \textbf{medietātem} means \emph{middle-ness}: the state of being in the middle. A half is what you get when you cut at the middle, so \emph{middle-ness} became \emph{a half}, and Spanish wore \emph{medietatem} down to \emph{mitad}.

English took \emph{medius} many ways: a \textbf{medium} is in the middle, a \textbf{median} splits a road, to \textbf{mediate} is to stand between. And English has the very same word as \emph{mitad}, though almost nobody uses it: \textbf{moiety} means a half, and came from \emph{medietatem} through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Numbers can now be broken as well as counted.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la mitad}
  \item \emph{la mitad del agua}
  \item \emph{una mitad y otra mitad}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two pieces make \emph{mitad}? (\emph{Medius}, middle, plus the \emph{-tātem} that gives \emph{-dad}.) And what does \emph{medietātem} mean word for word? (Middle-ness.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la docena]{la docena — the dozen, which is two and ten said quickly}

\label{lesson:ES-C344-docena}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the number}, then \emph{the half}. (\emph{El número}; \emph{la mitad}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco — where counting started.
  \item el número — the word for the count.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{do-SE-na}, the weight on the middle beat. The \emph{c} before \emph{e} is soft, and the \emph{d} is soft between vowels. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la docena} — \textquotedblleft{}the dozen,\textquotedblright{} a set of twelve.

Latin counted twelve as \textbf{duodecim} — \textbf{duo} \emph{two} plus \textbf{decem} \emph{ten}. Two and ten, said as one word, which is exactly how English says \emph{thirteen} and \emph{fourteen} but stops doing right before it reaches twelve.

Spanish wore \emph{duodecim} down to \textbf{doce}, and then added the ending \textbf{-ena}, which makes a group of that size. So \emph{docena} is \emph{a twelve-ful}, a set counted out by twelves.

English took the same Latin word by the French road and got \textbf{dozen}, which is \emph{duodecim} squashed nearly flat. Kept whole, it is \textbf{duodecimal} — counting in twelves, the system behind twelve inches, twelve months and twenty-four hours.

The \emph{duo} half is everywhere in English: a \textbf{duo}, a \textbf{duet}, a \textbf{duel} — and \textbf{double}, which is next.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A group can be counted as one thing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la docena}
  \item \emph{una docena}
  \item \emph{media docena}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{duodecim}, taken apart? (\emph{Duo} two plus \emph{decem} ten.) And what does the \emph{-ena} ending do? (Makes a group of that size.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[doble]{doble — double, which means folded in two}

\label{lesson:ES-C344-doble}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the half}, then \emph{the dozen}. (\emph{La mitad}; \emph{la docena}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la docena — the last of the counting words.
  \item la mitad — what this undoes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{DO-ble}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{b} is soft between vowels, made without quite closing the lips. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{doble} — \textquotedblleft{}double,\textquotedblright{} twice as much.

Latin \textbf{duplus} is \textbf{duo}, \emph{two}, plus \textbf{-plus}, which is a \emph{fold}. So \emph{duplus} is \emph{twofold} — and English \textbf{double} says the same thing by the same route, through French.

That \textbf{-plus} is a hidden joint in a great many words, and once you see it you cannot stop. \textbf{Triple} is threefold. \textbf{Multiple} is many-fold. \textbf{Simple} is \emph{sim-plus}, \textbf{onefold} — a thing with only one layer, which is why \emph{simple} means uncomplicated. English even has the plain Germanic version alongside: \emph{twofold}, \emph{threefold}, \emph{manifold}.

The two-fold has a dark side as well. \textbf{Duplicity} is being folded in two — having a second, hidden layer — which is precisely what we accuse a double-dealer of. A \textbf{duplex} has two folds of floor, and to \textbf{duplicate} is to make the second fold.

Against it stands \textbf{la mitad}, which cuts back to one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five counting words: \emph{cero}, \emph{el número}, \emph{la mitad}, \emph{la docena}, \emph{doble}. Nothing counted, halved or doubled is out of reach.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{doble}
  \item \emph{el doble}
  \item \emph{doble o mitad}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \emph{-plus} in \emph{duplus} mean? (A fold.) And what is \emph{simple}, taken apart? (\emph{Sim-plus} — onefold.)
\end{tcolorbox}
